Reach for a pure spin lock only where the holder cannot be preempted and sections are tiny, as in a kernel with preemption disabled. Reduce contention itself (shorter sections, or sharding: splitting the data into parts that each have their own lock) before tuning spin counts.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI has **false positives**. Not every dangerous structure is part of a real cycle, so some aborted transactions would have been fine. The paper reports serialization failure rates well under 1% on its benchmarks and an overall cost under 7% versus plain snapshot isolation, but your workload may differ.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Few labels, new domain, and the failure modes that remain
md: When labels are scarce, spend them on **measurement** first and **training** second. A few hundred carefully labelled lines plus a pile of noisily labelled ones beats a thousand rushed labels with no held-out set, because without a trustworthy eval you cannot tell whether any change helped.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
md: A perceptual hash finds copies of *the same picture*, not *pictures of the same thing*. Two different photos of the same dog get unrelated hashes. For semantic similarity you need learned embeddings: vectors that a trained neural network outputs for each image, placed so that images with similar content land close together (lesson 5 covers one built for copies).

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Colocated vs non-colocated generation, and how weights are refit
md: Colocated means no idle GPUs between phases but strictly sequential phases and careful memory handoffs; non-colocated means dedicated pools, a network refit (NCCL by default) and idle time unless you turn on async GRPO.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RST injection and the history of TCP session hijacking
md: Address-based trust is the real bug behind classic hijacking. Any system that grants access because a packet claims a source IP (old rsh, IP allow lists alone, zone transfers allowed by address) is relying on something an attacker can forge. Use cryptographic authentication.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: From overview to stream: the Wireshark workflow, decryption and tshark
md: A key log file is the key to every session it lists. Treat it like a password file: create it only for test traffic on your own machine, store it with the capture under the same protection, and delete both when done. Never set SSLKEYLOGFILE on a machine others use.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Extracting files from traffic: reassembly, true types and hashes
md: A hash lookup that returns nothing does not mean a file is safe: new and targeted malware is unknown by definition. Treat unknown executables from unusual sources as suspicious until analysed.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Routing: gateways, TTL, traceroute and BGP
md: Routing is decided hop by hop from tables, and the most specific matching prefix wins. On the internet those tables are built from announcements other networks make, which BGP accepts on trust unless someone filters or validates them.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: Reading is not touching. The `mbind(2)` man page notes that a first *read* of an anonymous page maps a shared page of zeros held by the kernel; no page is allocated on your node until the first *write*. A warm-up loop that only reads does not place anything.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Garbage collection and the write amplification formula
md: A drive does not know which LBAs your file system considers free. Unless told (lesson 4), every LBA ever written counts as live. Agrawal et al. put it bluntly: unlike a log-structured file system (one that, like an FTL, appends every write to a log and cleans it, but knows which files were deleted), the disk here is always full, so cleaning pressure is maximal all the time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
md: AP measures ranking quality across all thresholds for one class; COCO mAP averages it over 10 IoU thresholds and all classes. When comparing papers, check which one is reported: AP50 and AP@[.5:.95] differ a lot for the same model.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
md: Tiered storage moves *old* data to S3 and leaves the write path alone. S3-native moves the *write path itself* to S3, trading commit latency for stateless compute. Hybrids like Neon put a small quorum log in front so commits stay fast while object storage holds the bulk.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: Alert on symptoms, not causes. The SRE book's advice is to focus much more effort on catching symptoms than causes, and to worry about a cause only when it is very definite and very imminent. A page saying "cache hit rate dropped" is a cause; a page saying "users are burning the checkout budget at 20x" is a symptom, and it stays correct when the cause next time is something else.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
md: Layout-aware models add *where* to *what*: each word's box becomes embedding lookups, so a model can learn that a value sits right of its key. OCR-free models fold reading into the network and emit structure directly.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Linux capabilities: splitting root into pieces
md: `docker run --privileged` gives the container all capabilities and access to all host devices (Docker documentation). Treat it as running the workload as root on the host. The same goes for adding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or `CAP_SYS_MODULE` "just for one feature".

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
md: Red lines in this course: no locating, profiling or tracking of specific private individuals; no misrepresentation to get access; no use of credentials or data from breaches; no publishing of personal details. Worked examples use your own organisation, a fictional company (Northwind, under the reserved `.example` domain) or public institutions and already-public cases.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Metadata: what photos and documents say about themselves
md: Files describe themselves. Read metadata as one clue that needs corroboration; remove it from everything you publish.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
md: Check only your own accounts, or colleagues' with their consent. Looking up someone else's email in breach data or a broker profile, without a lawful basis, is exactly the profiling this course rules out.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Declare every real dependency on the target that uses it, with the narrowest correct scope: PRIVATE if only the .cpp files use it, PUBLIC if your headers expose it, INTERFACE if only your headers do. CMake then derives include paths, definitions and link order for you.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Do not add `@pytest.mark.flaky` or `xfail` to a test your PR broke. Maintainers read that as hiding a failure. If you believe a failure is pre-existing flakiness, show evidence: the same test failing on `main` or on other PRs, or a seed that reproduces it without your change.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: You may not add a Reviewed-by, Tested-by or Acked-by tag for someone just because they said nice things. The kernel guide says these need the named person's explicit permission; only Cc:, Reported-by: and Suggested-by: can be added with implicit permission.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Before using an AI tool on a contribution, find the project's policy (CONTRIBUTING, developer docs, or the docs on patch submission). Then: never submit what you cannot explain, disclose as the project asks, and never let a tool add your sign-off.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: `--force-with-lease` says "overwrite only if the remote is still what I last fetched". Add `--force-if-includes` so a fetch alone does not count as having seen the remote's commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: The most common CLA failure is an email mismatch: the commits use a personal or unregistered address while the agreement (or the employer's group) lists another. Fix the author email and rewrite the commits, not the agreement.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values
md: Significant is not the same as large. benchstat's docs stress that with enough low-noise data even very small changes become significant. Report the size of the change and its spread, and use the test only to answer "is this more than noise?"

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A bug report's first job is to let the maintainer make the failure happen themselves. Everything else in the report (description, guesses about the cause) comes second.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: A flaky repro is not done until it fails every time or you know its failure rate. Pin seeds and inputs, report versions, and repeat runs enough times that a PASS means something.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Self-review first, then mark ready. A reviewable PR is focused, explained, clean, and honestly labeled as draft or ready.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Prefix caching never changes outputs. It reuses KV for exactly the same tokens instead of recomputing it, so its effects are on speed and memory (outputs can differ only by the tiny floating-point noise any change in batching causes). It helps exactly as much as prefill dominates the work and prefixes repeat.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Verifying findings safely, without becoming the incident
md: Verify with the least risky evidence that answers the question. Write down the confidence and what you chose not to do. Stop immediately when you see signs that someone else got there first.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols
md: Missing callers, a detached tower over [unknown], or hex instead of names are not hot spots. They are profiler blind spots. Fix frame pointers or symbols before you trust the picture.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
md: The one thing to remember: phishing attacks a decision, not a machine. Defences therefore come in three kinds: stop the message arriving, make the action harmless if taken (for example passkeys, logins that only work on the real site; lesson 12), and make the final step need a second check (for example calling the supplier on a known number).

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Lookalike domains and homoglyphs
md: Misconception: "hover over the link and check the domain" solves this. A homoglyph domain can look correct even when you hover, and on phones you often cannot hover. Machine checks (skeletons, domain age) and phishing-resistant logins (lesson 12) carry the load; human checks are a backup.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Byte order: reading and writing multi-byte fields on the wire
md: Wire formats fix two things: where each field sits and the byte order inside it. Pick the order in the format's specification, then convert at the edge with shifts, `from_be_bytes` or `ntohl`, and keep ordinary structs inside the program.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
md: Keypoints are noisy, especially when occluded. Before writing rules on them: check per-keypoint visibility or score, prefer 3D world landmarks or a side view for sagittal angles (bends in the side-view plane that splits the body into left and right) such as the knee, smooth over a few frames, and use two thresholds (hysteresis) rather than one.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Crypto inventory and agility: finding every RSA before 2030
md: Agility has a price you met in tls-pki: anything that negotiates can be **downgraded**. Keep the allowed list short, remove algorithms rather than leaving them enabled "just in case", and authenticate the negotiation (as TLS 1.3 does by signing the transcript). An unauthenticated algorithm field is an attacker's choice, not yours.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: **The one thing to remember:** ask whether the next address is known before the current load finishes. If not, you are latency-bound and more bandwidth will not help. If yes, you are probably bandwidth-bound and the question becomes how many bytes you move.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Pseudonyms and hashes are not anonymity: AOL 2006
md: A hash of an identifier is an identifier. Anyone who can guess the input space (all phone numbers, all emails in a leaked list) can reverse it. Use a keyed HMAC for pseudonyms, and remember that pseudonymised data is still personal data.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy: a promise about one person
md: DP does not promise that nothing can be learned about you. If a study shows smoking causes cancer, a smoker's insurer learns something. DP promises that the result would have been about the same whether or not *your* data was in it.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Designing for less: data minimisation and purpose limitation
md: "We might need it later" is not a purpose. Data collected without a specified purpose fails GDPR Article 5(1)(b) and becomes an unreviewed liability in every copy.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy
md: Deleting the primary row is not erasure. Without a data map, copies in analytics, tickets, partners and backups survive, and the reply you sent the user is false.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket: why a hash works like a password
md: A hash or ticket is a password-equivalent. Protect where it is cached, make each one valid in as few places as possible, and watch for valid logons in the wrong context: right account, wrong machine, wrong protocol, wrong time.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: What should a step reward measure? Value, progress, implicit PRMs
md: Value says how promising a prefix is; progress (an advantage) says whether this step helped. Progress is the better step reward, if measured under a complementary prover. Implicit PRMs get Q values for free from an outcome model trained as a log ratio, and PRIME keeps that model fresh with online updates.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a context switch, step by step
md: Register save and restore is the same for every switch. The difference between a thread switch and a process switch is the address space: if `next` shares `prev`'s memory, the page table stays loaded and the TLB stays valid.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Distances from codes: lookup tables, SDC and ADC
md: ADC = exact query, quantized database. Per query you build an $m \times k^*$ table once, then each database vector costs $m$ lookups and adds. This is why PQ scans are fast and why everyone uses ADC.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Sequence recovery is a proxy, not a goal. A design that recovers 100 percent of a natural sequence has designed nothing new, and a design that recovers 30 percent may fold perfectly well. Recovery is useful only because it correlates with getting the physics right. What you actually test is whether the designed sequence folds back to the backbone you asked for.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Files, functions and exceptions: scripts that survive bad input
md: Read files with `with open(..., encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")`, put reusable steps in functions, and catch only the exceptions you can handle. A missing log is a finding, not a zero.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Safe coding habits: no eval, no shell strings, no secrets in code
md: Data is never code. Parse it with a format-specific parser, pass it to other programs as list arguments, validate it against what it should be, and keep secrets in the environment, not in the file.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
md: Misconception: the rewriter should make the query richer. Its job is to make it *standalone and faithful*. A rewriter that adds guessed facts (say, "when the leader fails during a network partition") can steer retrieval toward documents the user never asked about. Instruct it not to answer, and to return the message unchanged when it is already standalone.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
md: Per vector, the query-time work is a few AND plus popcount passes over the D-bit code and a handful of multiply-adds with precomputed factors. The error bound then tells you which candidates are worth an exact distance.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Race conditions from zero: concurrency, the race window and TOCTOU
md: A lock inside one process (threading.Lock here) protects only threads in that process. A web app with several worker processes or servers needs the lock where the state lives, usually in the database (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Why "too fast to exploit" fails: jitter and the single-packet attack
md: The single-packet attack made network distance irrelevant: a tester far away can now hit a 1 ms window about as reliably as one on the same network. Treat every check-then-act as reachable, and fix it with atomicity, not with speed.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
md: Stored on a majority is not the same as committed. An entry from an *earlier* term can sit on a majority and still be erased by a later leader. Commitment is only decided by counting replicas of an entry from the leader's *current* term, which then commits everything before it.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: What a ranker sees: one feature vector per query-document pair
md: A ranking model only knows what its feature vector tells it. If a signal that decides relevance (freshness for news, location for local search) is not encoded as a number for each query-document pair, no amount of model tuning can recover it.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: ERR: a user who stops once satisfied
md: **$g_{\max}$ is a convention, and tools hard-code it.** TREC's `gdeval.pl` (the official Web track script, which ir_measures used for `ERR@5` in our test) sets `MAX_JUDGMENT = 4`. With our 0 to 3 grades, gdeval gives Run A an ERR@5 of 0.240, not 0.452, and Run B 0.438, not 0.875. Rankings of runs may survive, but the numbers cannot be compared with an ERR computed under $g_{\max} = 3$.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Change Healthcare and ALPHV, February 2024
md: One remote access portal without MFA, at one subsidiary, gave a criminal nine quiet days. Inventory every remote access path (VPNs, Citrix, RDP gateways, vendor portals, acquired companies' systems) and enforce MFA on all of them, then test that it is enforced.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
md: An (address, rkey) pair is a capability: whoever holds it, on a QP in the same protection domain, can read or write that memory with no further check by your CPU. Grant the narrowest access flags you need, and revoke by deregistering (`ibv_dereg_mr`) or with memory windows, which the manual describes as a cheaper way to grant and revoke remote access dynamically.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Client-side prediction and server reconciliation
md: Each server state is a statement about the past: "here is the world after your input #n". Reset to it, then replay inputs after #n. Sequence numbers are what make that subtraction possible.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
md: Retrieval must be cheap per item (dot products over precomputed vectors); ranking can be expensive per item. In-batch negatives are sampled by popularity, so correct each logit by log p_j.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: A query plan is a tree of operators that pull rows
md: Cost units are not milliseconds. They are relative estimates the planner uses to compare plans. To see real time, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually runs the query.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
md: A commit is only as safe as the set of machines that had it when the client was told "ok". Every replication knob is a choice of *how many* and *which* machines that set must include, paid for in commit latency.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: What RLHF reward hacking looks like: length, sycophancy, persuasion
md: Misconception: longer answers after RLHF just mean a more helpful model. Sometimes length carries real information. But when the reward gain mostly vanishes once you compare answers of equal length, the policy has optimized a correlate of quality, not quality. Report output length next to every reward and win rate.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: A common misconception: "security owns security risk". In every framework in this course, the **business owner** of a system owns its risk and the decision to accept it. The security team advises, measures and challenges. When security silently accepts risk on the business's behalf, nobody with budget or authority knows the risk exists.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Treating risk: accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid
md: Every risk ends in one of four decisions, recorded with an owner and a date. Compare options in money: expected yearly loss plus treatment cost for the average, and tail percentiles for survival. Mitigation usually wins on average; insurance wins on the tail; avoidance can win on both.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: PCI DSS v4: the cardholder data environment and scoping
md: PCI DSS is a contractual standard with 12 requirements. Scope is the CDE plus anything connected to it or able to affect it, so reduce scope first: segment, and better, never touch card numbers (tokenise with a payment provider). What remains on your side, especially the payment page's scripts, must be inventoried and watched.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Policies people follow and awareness that works
md: Policies: short, owned, true, enforced by guardrails, with an exception path and a review date. Awareness: required by every framework, but measure it honestly; put the weight on controls that make human mistakes survivable, and on making reporting easy.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Colocated or disaggregated: where the engines live
md: Colocation trades memory and switch time for zero idle pools. Disaggregation trades network sync and staleness for overlap and freedom to size each pool. The long tail pushes large reasoning runs toward disaggregated, asynchronous designs.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Ceilings, hierarchical rooflines and Nsight Compute
md: Read the gaps. In the NERSC study of DeepCAM (a deep learning model that finds extreme weather patterns in climate images), a kernel whose L1, L2 and HBM points sit close together shows a streaming pattern with poor cache locality; a large gap between the L2 and HBM points shows that L2 misses were rare. The binding level is the one whose roof is lowest at that level's own intensity.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: At the default k = 60 with typical windows (tens of results), RRF behaves like a vote count first (how many lists returned the document) and uses ranks mainly to order documents with the same count. Smaller k gives ranks more say; larger k makes it closer to pure vote counting.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Build, load and test a Rust module
md: Misconception: "an `assert!` in a kernel doctest panics the kernel." In doctests and `#[kunit_tests]` modules the assert macros are replaced with versions that report to KUnit and do not panic. That is also why tests should use `?` instead of `unwrap()`: an `unwrap()` on `Err` is a real panic, and the kernel's panic handler calls `BUG()`, which reports a fatal kernel error (more in lesson 3).

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The baseline you replace: EEVDF picks and the knobs it offers
md: EEVDF in one line: weight sets the share, the requested slice sets the latency, and eligibility keeps any task from running far ahead of its share. A BPF scheduler gets none of this for free; lesson 5 shows the minimal one getting weights only partly right.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Build, load and run your own scheduler end to end
md: A scheduler is two programs: a BPF object (callbacks plus maps, gathered in one `sched_ext_ops` struct_ops map) and a loader that opens it, sets read-only options, loads, attaches, polls and reports why it exited. Exiting the loader is the unload.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
md: Measure percentiles, not means; A/B on one kernel, alternating runs, and report the spread. Then verify the nice and cgroup controls you depend on, because each scheduler decides which ones it honors.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Rotation without outages: overlap, versions and staged labels
md: Rotation that nobody watches fails silently. Alert on rotation failures, on keys older than their cryptoperiod, and on authentication failures right after a rotation (a consumer that missed the switch). The Storm-0558 key in the next lesson survived because rotation had stopped and nothing alerted on its age.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: archives, asserts, temp files and what Bandit sees
md: Python review checklist from lessons 3 and 4: no eval/exec/pickle/unsafe YAML on outside data; archive extraction with filter='data' and size limits; no assert for security; mkstemp or NamedTemporaryFile, never mktemp; secrets for tokens and compare_digest for comparisons; and a manual trace for every path.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Apple goto fail: one duplicated line in C
md: When reviewing C control flow, read the braces, not the indentation, and ask: if this function exits early, what does it return? A security check must fail closed: the only path to "success" should be the one that passed every check.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Writing the finding and the fix so it gets merged
md: A finding is complete when a developer can act on it alone: what is wrong (line and CWE), why it matters (impact and who can reach it), how you know (a safe reproduction), how to fix the class (code), and how to keep it fixed (a regression test that fails on the old code).

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Blast-RADIUS (CVE-2024-3596): MD5 collisions turn Reject into Accept
md: The bug was not "MD5 is old" alone. It was MD5 in a construction that let a collision survive the secret (secret at the end), plus a protocol rule that let the attacker plant bytes inside the authenticated reply. Keyed constructions like HMAC, and authenticating the whole channel with TLS, remove both.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Assurance: the Orange Book, Common Criteria and what they prove
md: "EAL4 certified" on a datasheet tells you how hard the evaluators looked, not what they looked at. The answer to "certified for what?" is in the security target, and it may exclude the very feature you are buying the product for.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: SASE, SSE and the cloud edge: SD-WAN, SWG, CASB and FWaaS
md: SASE is a delivery model, not a new control. Underneath it are the same enforcement points as before (firewall, web filter, CASB, ZTNA), moved from your data centre to someone else's points of presence.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: LLM-assisted triage: the model advises, code and people decide
md: A suggestion field that accepts free text will eventually contain an action, a threat or an instruction. Constrain it to a fixed set of values and treat everything else as a failed reply.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, payload and risk
md: Vulnerability = the weakness. Threat = who or what could use it. Exploit = the act or code that uses it. Payload = what runs afterwards. Risk = likelihood times impact. You remove risk by fixing vulnerabilities, reducing exposure, or reducing impact (backups, and segmentation: splitting a network into zones that cannot freely reach each other).

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Equifax 2017: a known bug and a missed patch
md: Equifax failed at the boring basics: inventory, patch tracking, credential storage, segmentation and monitoring health. No single failure caused the breach; every layer had a hole, which is the subject of lesson 10.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Plain, direct and first: sentences a busy reader acts on
md: Hedging is not the same as honesty. "May potentially" hides uncertainty instead of stating it. If you are unsure, say what you know, what you do not, and how sure you are (the incident lesson later in this course gives you the words). If you are sure, do not hedge to sound modest.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: The search policy is a better policy than the network that guided it. Training the network to imitate it is **policy improvement by imitation**. No human labels are used, but new information does enter the loop: from look-ahead, and from the game rules that score every finished game.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Using failures and training the judge: V-STaR, the gap, Meta-Rewarding
md: Training the judge on its own meta-judgments imports new biases. By iteration 2 the meta-judge preferred the judgment with the higher score 97.68% of the time, the judge's mean score rose from 4.1 to over 4.7 out of 5, and position bias grew. Scores bunched near the top, which made responses harder to tell apart. Lesson 6 flagged the same risk: a judge's blind spots become the policy's target.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Compression has costs of its own. The compressor runs on the critical path of every request. The compressed text is hard for humans to read, which makes debugging and audits harder. Exact strings (code, JSON, numbers, IDs) can be damaged by token deletion. And question-aware compression produces a different context for every question, so that context can no longer be served from the provider's prefix cache.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell: how logging a string ran code
md: Only `log4j-core` 2.x is affected; applications with just `log4j-api` are not, and Log4j 1.x has no lookups (its separate JMSAppender issue is CVE-2021-4104). But Log4j is often a *transitive* dependency: a library you use pulls it in, so "we do not use Log4j" needs checking, not assuming.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
md: Cache locality and load balance pull against each other. Sending every request of a hot prefix to one worker maximizes hits and can overload that worker; the balance thresholds exist to break locality when queues diverge. The gateway's trees are approximate: they are inferred from routed text, not read from the workers, so they can be stale.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: No technique wins on every axis. Look at query time, preprocessing time, memory, how quickly new traffic weights can be applied, and whether turns and other metrics are supported. A static fastest-route server and a live-traffic service often choose differently.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
md: Every hand-written SIMD loop has a vector body, a horizontal reduction and a tail. A vector reduction adds in a different order than the scalar loop, so float results can change, which is why compilers need permission to reassociate.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: "Arena" means different things in different allocators. In this lesson it is a bump region freed all at once. In jemalloc (a general-purpose malloc used by FreeBSD and Firefox, among others) and in glibc malloc (the GNU C library's allocator, the default on most Linux systems) an *arena* is an independent general-purpose heap with its own locks, used so threads contend less; you still free objects one by one there.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
md: The colocated code keeps a comment worth remembering: SGLang returns from the update request after enqueueing GPU copies, not after they finish. Reusing the same flattened IPC buffer for the next bucket right away could overwrite memory SGLang is still reading and corrupt weights, so slime allocates a fresh buffer per bucket.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Enrichment: asset, identity and intel context, and where it lies
md: Enrichment answers "what is this thing?", not "is this bad?". Treat every enriched field as a claim with a source and an age, show unknowns explicitly, and never let a single reputation score close or escalate an alert by itself.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Talking to users, owners and leaders during an investigation
md: Never let an attacker-controlled message decide who you trust. A chat message saying "I'm from IT, please approve the prompt" is exactly what the Lapsus$ actors sent, per the CSRB. The same rule applies inside the SOC: verify urgent requests to disable monitoring or grant access through a second channel.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Designing help-desk verification that holds under pressure
md: Misconception: "on-camera verification solves help-desk fraud". It raises the bar, but synthetic video and stolen ID images are already used against identity checks (FinCEN, 2024). Pair it with an out-of-band confirmation for anything privileged, and keep the most powerful admin accounts out of help-desk reach entirely.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: An SAE is dictionary learning with a neural network: an encoder that picks a few latents, a decoder whose columns are the dictionary directions, and a loss that trades reconstruction against sparsity.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: Judge an SAE by sparsity (L0), reconstruction (FVU) and downstream loss together, then verify interpretations causally. Steering by clamping a latent equals adding $(c - f_i)$ times its decoder direction while keeping the SAE error.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
md: An empirical variogram from a handful of points is very noisy, and the fitted range and nugget can swing a lot with the bin edges or the fitting weights. Look at the plot, try a second binning and treat the parameters as uncertain, not as measured truths.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
md: A common bug: after a rejection, keeping the target's distributions for later positions. Those were computed with the rejected guess in the context, so they condition on a token that is no longer in the output. Only the distribution at the first rejected position is valid.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
md: Whisper is an audio-conditioned language model. The encoder turns 30 s of log-mel into 1500 vectors; the decoder generates the transcript token by token, with language, task and timestamps expressed as tokens in the same sequence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: Stack memory lives exactly as long as the function call that created it. Allocation and release are a pointer adjustment, which is why the size must be bounded and why anything that must outlive the call has to go somewhere else: the heap.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: TLB reach = entries x page size. Working sets beyond it pay a page walk on most random accesses; huge pages raise reach by 512 times, and every unmap in a multithreaded process may interrupt other CPUs.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Lab: build, sweep and evaluate a steering vector on a small chat model
md: Three things bite first attempts. The chat template inserts a default system prompt ("You are Qwen...") when you give none. Qwen's tokenizer turns "(A" into a single token, so the answer letter is not a separate position: read activations at the "(A" token and score the "(A" and "(B" tokens. And the hook must cope with both output types of a decoder layer. Print the tokens of one full prompt before anything else.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Watermark = the processor's estimate of how far event time has progressed. It decides when a window first fires; allowed lateness decides how long the window can still be corrected; anything beyond is dropped or side-output. Every choice trades latency for completeness.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, teacher forcing and cross-attention
md: A causal mask sets the scores of future positions to minus infinity before softmax, so with teacher forcing every target position trains in one pass without seeing its own answer. Cross-attention is the same function with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: "Transformer" does not mean "GPT" (generative pre-trained transformer, OpenAI's line of decoder-only language models). The 2017 model is an encoder-decoder for translation. Decoder-only language models keep only its masked self-attention stack; encoder-only models keep only the unmasked encoder.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
md: Training is **teacher forcing on every position in parallel**: the true previous tokens are always the context, and all $B \times T$ predictions are scored in one pass. Generation is the opposite, one token at a time feeding its own outputs back in.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
md: The model never stores the text it generated anywhere except in `idx`. There is no hidden memory across calls: anything older than `block_size` tokens is simply cropped away and cannot influence the next prediction.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
md: The gradient points in the direction of **steepest ascent**, and its length is that steepest rate. So $-\nabla f$ is the direction of steepest descent, the direction every gradient-based **optimizer** (the algorithm that updates the parameters during training) starts from.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation: the chain rule run backward through a graph
md: Gradient checks can fail for honest reasons: at a kink (a sharp corner) such as ReLU at 0 (lesson 2) or a max with ties, the function is not differentiable and the two sides disagree. Check at random points away from kinks, and in double precision.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
md: Misconception: `2>&1` *links* stderr to stdout permanently. It does not. It is a one-time copy of fd 1 as it is at that moment. Any later change to fd 1 leaves fd 2 where it was.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Job control and signals: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, background jobs and trap
md: Ctrl-C is SIGINT, Ctrl-Z is SIGTSTP, `kill` is SIGTERM, `kill -9` is SIGKILL, and a closed terminal is SIGHUP. In a script, route every way out, signals included, through one `trap ... EXIT` cleanup.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Evaluating and visualizing an embedding space
md: A t-SNE plot shows neighbourhoods, not geometry. Do not conclude that one cluster is more varied than another, or that two clusters are closer than a third, from the picture. Check such claims with distances computed in the original space.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Doubling peak TFLOP/s does almost nothing for batch-1 decode. What helps is moving fewer bytes per token (smaller or quantized weights: quantizing stores each weight in fewer bits, so 8-bit weights halve the bytes) or using each byte for more tokens (batching, next lessons).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
md: Misconception: "signed overflow wraps in C too." The hardware adder wraps, but in C, overflowing a signed integer is [undefined behavior](https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/language/operator_arithmetic), and compilers optimize on the assumption that it never happens. Only unsigned arithmetic is guaranteed to wrap modulo $2^n$.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
md: Performance is often decided by memory access patterns, not instruction counts. Touch memory sequentially, reuse data while it is still in cache, and keep hot data small.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline
md: Raw crawl becomes training data through extraction, filtering, near-duplicate removal, PII and contamination handling, then packing. Each step was chosen by training small models on the result, and a run then moves through stages: main pretraining, context extension, annealing.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
md: RLHF does not maximize reward. It maximizes reward minus beta times the KL from the SFT model, and beta sets how far the model may move to chase the reward model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
md: The vector space model scores a document by the cosine between its tf-idf vector and the query's. Engines compute it by streaming the query terms' postings into accumulators, so documents that share no query term cost nothing.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Multi-file C: headers, include guards, static, extern and make
md: Headers hold declarations (`extern` variables, prototypes) behind an include guard; exactly one .c file holds each definition; `static` keeps helpers private. A Makefile lists what each file depends on, and make rebuilds only what is older than its inputs.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Before you keep a pointer, ask how long the object behind it lives. Locals die when their function returns, malloc'd memory dies at free, and realloc can retire the old address at any call.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
md: Develop C with `-Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined` on, and fix every warning. Most of the pointer and lifetime bugs from this course then fail loudly at the exact line instead of corrupting memory silently.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: Shared XOR mutable: any number of `&T`, or exactly one `&mut T`, never both at the same point in the program. A borrow is live from creation to last use.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
md: Default to borrowing; move when the callee should keep the value; clone when copies are cheap or necessary; use `Rc`/`RefCell` only for data with genuinely shared ownership.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: $A\mathbf{x}$ is both a stack of dot products (one per row) and a weighted sum of columns. The columns of $A$ are the images of the basis vectors, so they fully describe the map.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Tensors, batches and broadcasting: shapes in real code
md: Broadcasting checks sizes, never meaning. A loss computed from (3, 1) predictions and (3,) targets averages 9 differences instead of 3 and raises nothing. Assert shapes where arrays from different places meet: `assert pred.shape == y.shape`.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
md: With many features, predictions are $\hat y = Xw$ and the MSE gradient is $\frac{2}{n}X^\top(Xw - y)$. Its minimum solves the normal equations $X^\top Xw = X^\top y$. Features on very different scales stretch the bowl, so gradient descent crawls; standardizing them rounds it out.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Validation and penalties: choosing lambda, L2 and L1
md: Choose capacity and penalty strength by **validation** error and keep the test set for one final check. L2 (weight decay) shrinks every weight a little each step; L1 pins weak weights at exactly zero and so selects features.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: Misconception: a deeper network of linear layers is more expressive. It is not; it is exactly as expressive as one linear layer. Another one: universal approximation means any network will learn any function. It only guarantees that suitable weights exist.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradients through depth: vanishing, exploding and unlucky seeds
md: Backprop computes the exact gradient of the loss at the current weights; it does not guarantee a good solution. The loss surface of a network is not **convex** (bowl-shaped, so that every valley is the lowest one), so the starting point matters. Lesson: always check the loss curve, and try more than one seed.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
md: Memory is a cache for pages, and a disk-backed miss costs about 100,000 memory accesses. A replacement policy tries to approximate OPT using the past: LRU in principle, the use bit and the clock algorithm in practice, preferring clean pages.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: how a hard disk spends its time
md: A random disk I/O is almost all positioning: seek plus half a rotation, milliseconds, against microseconds of transfer. Make requests large and sequential, and let the scheduler order them by position.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Conditioning means restricting attention to the outcomes consistent with what you know, then renormalizing so they sum to 1. Almost every formula in this course is that one idea applied carefully.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
md: Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and sunburns are correlated because sunny weather drives both: a **confounder**, a third variable that causes both. The Deep Learning textbook by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville makes the same point about conditioning: P(from Germany | speaks German) is high, but teaching someone German does not change where they are from.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
md: Power depends on the effect size you assume. Choose the smallest effect worth acting on before you see data, not the effect you hope for and not the effect a finished test happened to show.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
md: A scaling study is an experiment design problem: budgets spread over orders of magnitude, sizes that bracket each valley, a properly ended schedule per run, then two fits (IsoFLOP parabolas and the parametric form) that should agree, each with bootstrap error bars.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
md: nDCG@k answers: what fraction of the best achievable discounted gain did the top k results capture? It is the default when labels are graded and users look mostly at the first page.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
md: Each stage covers another's blind spot: BM25 for rare exact terms, the bi-encoder for meaning across different words, the cross-encoder for precise final ordering on a short list. Evaluate the whole pipeline on your own queries with a metric such as recall at k (the share of relevant passages that appear in the top k results).

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Build a byte-level BPE tokenizer in Python
md: Decode with `errors="replace"` (or keep bytes) whenever ids can be cut at arbitrary points: one token at a time while streaming, or a sequence the model generated that may not be valid UTF-8. With strict decoding a partial character raises an error. When streaming, keep the bytes and only show the characters once all their bytes have arrived.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Residual connections: why 56 layers trained worse than 20
md: A residual block computes $x + F(x)$. The identity path makes doing nothing easy to learn and gives the gradient a direct route to every layer. Start each branch near zero so that a deep stack begins as one identity map rather than a variance amplifier.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude fewer distance computations. Every ANN number you read (or report) should come as a pair: recall@k and speed, measured against exact brute-force results on the same queries.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Version ranges and lockfiles: why new code arrives unasked
md: A lockfile only protects installs that use it. A Dockerfile that copies only package.json, `npx some-tool`, a global install, or a developer running `npm update` all resolve ranges fresh. The axios post-mortem told users who were "pinned to a clean version" and ran no fresh install in the window that they were fine.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
md: The xz attack was a trust attack, not a technical exploit of git, signing or builds. Every step was done by a legitimate maintainer with legitimate rights. Defences are partly social: fund and share maintenance of critical projects, add second reviewers for releases, and treat sudden pressure to hand over control or upgrade fast as a warning sign.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
md: Synthetic data are useful when an outside signal decides what is kept, diversity is designed in, and real data stay in the training mix. Model collapse is what happens when all three are missing.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR
md: Every `read` and `write` may block, move fewer bytes than asked, or fail with `EINTR` or `EAGAIN`. Loop until all bytes are moved, retry on `EINTR`, and treat `EAGAIN` as "wait until the descriptor is ready".

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
md: strace shows which calls a program makes and how often; getrusage shows the page faults that strace cannot see; seccomp turns a list of needed calls into an enforced allow-list. All three work on syscall numbers and miss the vDSO.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
md: A relative expression has no value until it is anchored. *Present*, *now*, *today*, *last year* and *the past 5 years* all need a reference date, and the normalizer should receive it as an explicit input, never read a hidden clock or let a model guess it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
md: Coverage is an **upper bound** on accuracy. It equals real accuracy only if you have a perfect checker (unit tests, a proof checker). For a math word problem, pass@100 = 83% means 83% of problems have *some* correct sample, not that you can find it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Do not assume more thinking tokens never hurt. Evaluate a reasoning model at several reasoning lengths on your own tasks. Wasted tokens on easy prompts (overthinking) and how to train them away are the subject of the efficient-reasoning course, a follow-on to this one.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
md: Titans' memory update = gradient descent with momentum (carry surprise forward) and weight decay (forget), all gated per token. Momentum keeps writing after a surprising event; forgetting keeps a fixed-size memory from overflowing.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay
md: A per-CPU or per-thread cache is a deliberate trade of memory for scalability. Idle rounds look like a leak in heap profiles and in RSS (resident set size, the physical memory a process currently holds), and they multiply by the number of CPUs (or threads) and caches. Every production design pairs its caches with a sizing policy and a way to give memory back.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: From hunt to detection: the FireEye countermeasures
md: Hunts and detections are two ends of one pipeline. Precise, low-volume hunts become alerts; noisy but valuable ones become scheduled hunts with an owner and a review rhythm, like FireEye's supplemental rules. A hunt that never feeds detection leaves the organisation exactly as blind as before, once the hunter moves on.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The Diamond Model: one event, four corners
md: Two traps. First, Type 2 infrastructure is what victims usually see, so an IP address's owner is often another victim, not the adversary. Second, a shared feature is a lead, not a link: two events that share a widely used tool are not necessarily the same adversary (the attribution lesson returns to this).

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
md: Do not let one view take over. The Threat Modeling Manifesto lists *tendency to overfocus* as an anti-pattern: avoid exaggerating attention on adversaries, assets, or techniques. A model built only around a feared attacker misses dull, likely failures.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
md: Compliance is not security. The Senate timeline notes that Target was certified compliant with PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, the card industry's security rules) in September 2013, two months before the breach. An audit checks controls at a moment; a threat model asks how an attacker would get from here to there.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A random train/test split on a time series leaks the future into training and makes every model look better than it will be in production. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos state the rule plainly: the training set may contain only observations that occurred before the test observations, so no future observations are used to construct the forecast.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
md: Downgrade defence has two halves: **authenticate the negotiation** (transcript signatures, the sentinel, SCSV) and **delete the weak options** so there is nothing to downgrade to. The second is the one that always works.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: A Triton program instance is not one thread. It is closer to a CUDA thread block: one program becomes `num_warps` warps of 32 threads each, so with the default `num_warps=4` a single program runs on 128 threads.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
md: The rule that keeps any mask honest: a position may only attend to what will exist when it is generated. Bidirectional attention inside an image is legal exactly when the whole image is produced together, as in diffusion, flow or masked prediction. Under token-by-token generation it would leak the answer.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Running an unmodified binary on a unikernel does not get you function-call costs. Trapping and translating each `syscall` cost 84 cycles in Unikraft's measurement, 21 times a function call. Relinking against the libOS is what removes the crossing.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: The spectrum: Linux-based unikernels, microVMs and sandboxes
md: Unikernel gains split into **removing the crossing** (small for real applications, per Lupine) and **specializing** (large). Linux can deliver much of the second. Choose a libOS unikernel when you also want tiny images, millisecond boots and a minimal attack surface, and can accept its limits.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
md: Durability comes from the log, not the index: indexes are rebuilt or replayed from the WAL. Speed comes from what fits in RAM: keep the navigation data (graph upper layers, compressed vectors) in memory, and make every disk read count.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and running verl in practice
md: verl in one sentence: a single Python controller expresses the RL algorithm as calls on WorkerGroups; each WorkerGroup runs a training or inference engine SPMD on a resource pool; DataProto carries the batch between them; and actor and rollout share GPUs by resharding or sleeping instead of keeping two copies.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
md: A video world model is three choices: how frames become latents (VQ tokens or continuous), how actions enter (logged, learned latent codes, or text), and how the next frame is sampled (masked token decoding or diffusion). All of them pay for autoregression with drift and finite memory, and they are judged on fidelity (FVD, human studies) and on control (delta PSNR).

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts
md: A VLA is a VLM whose output vocabulary also contains actions. Predicting the robot's next move becomes one more question the model answers, so the whole web-pretrained network is reused for control.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Codebook collapse: measuring and fixing unused codes
md: Track usage and perplexity during tokenizer training. A 16,384-entry codebook with perplexity 500 behaves like a much smaller vocabulary and wastes embedding rows in every downstream model.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: CUDA graphs: padding, support levels and mode downgrades
md: Graph capture assumes `forward` does the same thing at replay as at capture. That is why `AttentionImpl.forward` must not branch on Python values that change per batch inside a full graph, and why builders write into persistent buffers instead of allocating new tensors.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Reading a receipt into validated JSON
md: Do not ask the model to fill in a missing total by computing it. Then the arithmetic check compares the model with itself and can never fail.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: A practical wait-free queue: phases and helping (Kogan-Petrank)
md: Two checks in `help_enq` look redundant but are not. The paper shows that replacing `while (isStillPending(tid, phase))` with `while (true)` breaks wait-freedom, and dropping the second `isStillPending` check just before the CAS on `last.next` breaks linearizability, because a thread that was suspended there could insert a node another helper already inserted.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Foundation models, hybrids, and where these models break
md: "Foundation model" here does not mean a chatbot for weather. It means one pretrained network whose weights are reused and fine-tuned across forecasting tasks.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authorization at scale: two accounts and a replay matrix
md: If a replay ever returns another person's real data, stop. Do not page through more records to measure the scale. The disclose.io terms ask researchers to limit data access to the minimum needed for a proof of concept and to cease testing and report immediately when they encounter user data.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: How a page loads: HTML, subresources, JavaScript and the DOM
md: A script runs with the authority of **the page that includes it**, not the server it came from. `lib.js` from `cdn.example.net` runs as if `shop.example.com` had written it: it can read and change the shop's DOM, read the shop's visible cookies and send requests to the shop with the user's cookies. Including a script is handing over your keys.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Subresource Integrity and the trust you hand to third-party scripts
md: SRI only works for files that never change between requests. It cannot pin a script that is generated per request or a library loaded as "latest". Pin exact versions, self-host what you can, and keep the list of third-party scripts on sensitive pages (login, payment) as short as possible.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Event IDs that tell an intrusion story: 4688, 4720, 7045, 1102
md: Turn on command-line logging for 4688 (or deploy Sysmon). Without it you know rundll32.exe ran, but not what it was told to do, and that is usually the part that matters.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Rogue access points, evil twins and how enterprises find them
md: An evil twin of an *open* network is indistinguishable from the real one at the Wi-Fi layer: there is nothing to authenticate. Users on open or OWE networks must rely on TLS (lesson 9) for everything that matters.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Lockdown Mode, stalkerware and tracker abuse
md: For someone being monitored by an abuser, every defensive step can also alert the abuser: monitoring stopping, a tracker going silent. Technical help here should follow the person's own safety plan, ideally with a domestic violence support service, not just maximise security.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Run it yourself: one stable trunk, three cooldown branches
md: Branch checklist: weights, optimizer state (including its step count), the global step that drives the LR schedule, and the data position. A loss spike on the first step of a branch means the optimizer state was not restored; a branch that starts with a warmup means the step counter was reset.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: MSG_ZEROCOPY: sending from your own memory safely
md: A notification means "the kernel has released your pages", **not** "the data was delivered". With a deferred copy it can arrive before the copied data is even transmitted. Never use it as a transmit or delivery acknowledgement.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds
md: The perfect F1 at 0.6 comes from 12 decisions on 3 hand-picked texts. A threshold tuned on so few examples is overfit. Use hundreds of labeled examples, and keep a separate test split to report the final number.
